client: I've been really struggling since my dad passed away two months ago — it was so sudden, and I just wasn't prepared for any of it. Everything feels kind of gray and hollow now, like I go through the motions of my day but nothing actually feels meaningful anymore. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try something because I can't keep going on like this.
therapist: I'm really glad you reached out, and I want you to know that what you're carrying right now — this sudden loss, this grayness — makes complete sense given how abrupt and unprepared this all was. That hollowness you're describing, going through the motions without anything feeling real, is a very common and painful part of grief, and it doesn't mean something is permanently broken in you. I'm curious — when you say nothing feels meaningful anymore, are there any small moments, even brief ones, where that gray lifts even just a little?

client: Honestly, I had to think hard about that question, and maybe there are a couple of tiny moments — like when my dog comes and sits with me in the morning, or when I'm cooking something and I'm focused enough that my mind goes quiet for a bit. But it almost feels wrong to admit that, like if I say something felt okay, even for a second, I'm somehow betraying my dad or pretending this isn't as bad as it is. So I kind of push those moments away instead of letting myself have them.
therapist: What you just described is such an important insight — those quiet moments with your dog or while cooking aren't a betrayal of your dad, they're actually your mind and body finding tiny ways to keep you going, which takes real strength. Grief doesn't require you to be in pain every single second to prove that your love for him was real. I'm wondering, what do you think your dad would say if he knew you were pushing those small moments of peace away?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, because honestly, my dad was not the type to want anyone suffering on his behalf — he was always telling me to stop worrying so much and just enjoy things. So logically I know he'd probably tell me to let myself have those moments. But there's this other part of me that feels like accepting any peace right now means I'm starting to move on, and moving on feels like I'm leaving him behind, and I'm not ready for that at all.
therapist: It's really moving that you know your dad so well — you can almost hear his voice telling you to let yourself breathe, and that connection to who he was is actually a beautiful thing to hold onto. What I want to gently offer is this: allowing yourself a moment of peace isn't the same as moving on or leaving him behind — it's actually possible to carry him with you *and* still let yourself feel okay sometimes, and those two things don't have to cancel each other out. What does "leaving him behind" look like in your mind — is there a specific fear underneath that, like forgetting him, or something else?

client: I think the fear is that my memory of him will just... fade, like the details will get blurry over time and I'll forget the sound of his voice or the specific way he laughed, and then it'll be like he's really gone in a way that feels permanent. And if I stop being in pain, I'm afraid that's when the forgetting starts, like the grief is somehow keeping him present. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but it feels very real.
therapist: It doesn't sound irrational at all — it sounds like a mind that loves someone deeply and is trying to protect that connection in the only way it can figure out right now. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: the grief isn't actually what's keeping him present — *you* are, through your memories, the way you know exactly what he would have said just now, the things he taught you about enjoying life. What's one specific memory or detail about him — his laugh, a phrase he used — that feels vivid and alive to you right now, just to notice that it's still there?

client: He used to say "don't borrow trouble from tomorrow" whenever I'd spiral into worrying about things, and I can hear his voice saying it pretty clearly right now, which is... actually surprising, and a little painful at the same time. It's like you're right that the memory is there without me having to be in constant pain to access it, and that's kind of unsettling to realize. I'm not sure I'm ready to fully accept what that means yet, because it feels like it might take away the one reason I've been letting myself just feel terrible.
therapist: That phrase he gave you — "don't borrow trouble from tomorrow" — is alive in you right now, in his voice, and that's not nothing, that's actually profound. It makes complete sense that this realization feels unsettling, even a little threatening, because it means the pain isn't the only thread connecting you to him — and letting go of pain as a *purpose* is its own kind of loss that deserves to be grieved too. You don't have to fully accept anything today, but I'm curious — what might it feel like to just sit with the possibility that he can stay close to you even as you slowly, gently, start to feel a little less terrible?

client: Sitting with that possibility feels... I don't know, fragile maybe, like if I hold it too tight or examine it too closely it'll fall apart and I'll be back to feeling like the grief is all I have left of him. I guess I could try to just let that idea exist without deciding what to do with it yet, but I'm honestly a little scared that if I start allowing myself to feel better, I'll lose momentum and just pretend everything is fine when it isn't. I don't want to use this as an excuse to bury everything either, because I've done that before with hard things and it never actually works.
therapist: That self-awareness you just showed is really significant — you already know the difference between genuine relief and burying things, and that knowledge is actually a protection against the pattern you're afraid of repeating. There's a real middle path here that's neither "pretend everything is fine" nor "stay in pain to stay connected," and it sounds like you're already beginning to feel your way toward it, even if it feels fragile right now. What would it look like for you to keep grieving honestly *and* allow those small moments of peace — is there a way those two things could coexist in your day, even in a small way?

client: Maybe those two things could coexist, like letting myself have the quiet moment with my dog in the morning without immediately feeling guilty about it, and then also not running from it when the grief hits later in the day. But I'm worried that in practice, when I'm actually in those moments, I won't remember any of this clarity — I'll just feel the guilt and pull back like I always do. I guess I'm wondering if there's something more concrete I could do to actually hold onto this in the moment, because right now it feels more like an idea than something I know how to actually live.
therapist: What you're describing is such a real and common gap between insight and the actual moment — and the good news is that's exactly where small, concrete anchors can help. One thing that might bridge that gap is creating a simple reminder tied to those moments themselves — something like a short phrase you write down and keep nearby, even just your dad's own words: "don't borrow trouble from tomorrow," which could gently remind you in that morning moment with your dog that peace and love can exist at the same time. Would something like that feel worth trying this week — and is there a form that reminder might take that would actually feel meaningful to you rather than just like a task?

client: Writing down his phrase actually feels like something I could do without it feeling like a therapy exercise, because it's his words and not just some generic positive affirmation, so there's something real attached to it. I'm thinking maybe I could put it somewhere I'd actually see it, like near where I make my coffee in the morning, which is usually when the guilt hits hardest. I'm still a little skeptical that seeing a piece of paper is going to override how I feel in those moments, but I think I'm willing to try it because it at least feels connected to him rather than disconnected from all of this.
therapist: There's something really meaningful in the fact that this doesn't feel like a generic exercise to you — it feels like *him*, and that connection is exactly what makes it more likely to actually work in those hard morning moments. Your skepticism is completely fair, and I'd actually encourage you to hold onto it, because this isn't about a piece of paper magically overriding your feelings — it's about giving yourself a half-second pause where his voice gets to show up before the guilt takes over. How do you think you'll feel next week when you come back and tell me how those mornings went — is there a part of you that's quietly a little hopeful?

client: Yeah, I think there is a small part of me that's quietly hopeful, which is actually a weird feeling to notice because I haven't felt anything close to hopeful in two months. I'm almost suspicious of it, like I don't want to set myself up and then have a really bad week and feel like I failed at grief on top of everything else. But I guess I can try to just let the hope be small and not put too much weight on it, the same way I'm trying to let the peaceful moments just exist without analyzing them to death.
therapist: That small, quiet hope you're noticing is worth honoring — and the fact that you're already applying the same gentle approach to it, not gripping it too tightly, shows how much you've actually shifted just in this conversation. There's no such thing as failing at grief, and a hard day next week wouldn't undo any of this — it would just be a hard day, and those are allowed to exist alongside the hopeful ones. Be kind to yourself the way your dad would have been, and I'll look forward to hearing how those mornings go.

client: That last part you said, about being kind to myself the way my dad would have been, actually hit harder than I expected and I'm sitting here trying not to cry. I think I needed someone to frame it that way, because I'm much better at imagining how he'd treat me than figuring out how to treat myself. I'm going to try to hold onto that this week, even though I know there will probably be moments where it all feels impossible again.
therapist: The tears make complete sense — you just touched something really true about yourself, and that kind of recognition can be both painful and quietly healing at the same time. The fact that you can access his kindness so naturally is a gift, and this week, when treating yourself feels impossible, you don't have to figure out self-compassion from scratch — you can just ask what he would do, and let that be enough. You've done something really courageous today, and I'm genuinely glad you decided to try something.
